summary:
Stratum-4D is an interactive web tool that turns students and curious members of the public into Earth-system trend detectives. It shows 30 major river and ice basins on a 3D globe and loads 22 years (2002–2024) of NASA GRACE/GRACE-FO satellite measurements of how much water each basin holds. For every basin it answers the challenge's four questions: what is changing, where, how fast, and whether the change is real or just noise.

Behind a plain-language interface sits a solid statistics pipeline. It removes the seasons from each series, fits Theil-Sen slopes with 95% confidence intervals, and runs a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation. It then controls the false-discovery rate across all 30 basins and finds the year each trend broke. A three-question wizard, a guided tour and case files give newcomers a place to start. A click-anywhere probe pulls 40 years of NASA POWER climate data for any spot on Earth, and live NASA EONET and GIBS layers add context. Modelled series are clearly labelled as modelled.
details:
https://stratum-4d.vercel.app

Stratum-4D lets anyone play trend detective with the Earth's water. It maps 30 major river and ice basins and, for each one, answers the challenge's four questions in plain words: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. From 22 years of NASA GRACE/GRACE-FO data, 27 of the 30 basins show a significant trend (15 drying, 12 wetting, FDR q < 0.05). For the other 3 the tool answers "Not yet" instead of forcing a verdict.

The tool has four main parts:

• Three linked views: a 3D WebGL globe (Three.js with custom GLSL shaders), a flat 2D map showing all 30 basins at once, and a subsurface cut-away that illustrates what a trend means underground. The cut-away is a modelled illustration and is labelled as one.

• NASA data at the core: observed GRACE/GRACE-FO water storage (JPL RL06.1M mascons, 2002–2024); NASA POWER (MERRA-2) reanalysis for temperature, rainfall and root-zone soil moisture; six NASA GIBS imagery layers on the globe; and the live NASA EONET natural-event feed.

• Probe any point: click anywhere on Earth and the app pulls 41 years (1984–2024) of monthly NASA POWER data for that spot and runs the trend tests live in the browser.

• Compare regions: two basins side by side, with lagged correlations (0–12 months) and partial correlations against NOAA climate indices (ENSO, Indian Ocean Dipole, NAO). These show association, not proof of cause, and the app says so. Of our 8 preset pairs, 3 trend in opposite directions.

Straight-line regression can overstate significance on Earth-science series, because seasons and month-to-month persistence make data points less independent than they look. Each series therefore goes through:

1. STL (LOESS) seasonal decomposition and Yue-Pilon (2002) trend-free pre-whitening.

2. A Mann-Kendall test with the Hamed-Rao (1998) variance correction and effective sample size (n*).

3. Theil-Sen median slopes with 95% confidence intervals, compared with an ordinary least-squares t-test.

4. Benjamini-Hochberg (1995) false-discovery-rate control across all 30 basins.

5. Pettitt (1979) break years and Weatherhead et al. (1998) detection horizons, which estimate how much longer a record must be before a weak trend can be confirmed.

Groundwater and ice loss cannot be seen from the ground, and headlines rarely show how sure the science is. Stratum-4D lets students and the public check for themselves, and teaches the habit that matters most in trend analysis: asking "is it real?" before "how big?". Learners get a Plain | Technical wording switch, plain-language definitions of the variables, a three-question start (region type, what is changing, time window), a 12-lesson guided tour, a 90-second demo and case studies drawn from published research. Advanced users get water-year and flow-duration views and CSV export.

The project is creative in four ways:

• Answers first: every region opens on four plain sentences, with the full statistics one click away.

• "Not significant" is treated as a result worth showing, not hidden.

• Every series is labelled Observed, Reanalysis, Satellite imagery or Modelled proxy, so nobody mistakes an illustration for a measurement.

• One trend, three ways to see it: on the globe, on a flat map and underground.

In building it, our team considered:

• Audience: the challenge names students, so plain language comes first and jargon is opt-in.

• Honesty: measured and modelled data are separated everywhere, and every written summary is labelled as either a fixed template or AI-generated (optional OpenRouter model).

• Validity: autocorrelation and multiple testing are handled before any trend is called significant.

• Access: no API keys or accounts needed; the core analysis runs from data shipped with the app (live NASA layers need a connection). Text is at least 11 px with contrast of at least 5.6:1, and every dialog works from the keyboard.

• Limits: 30 fixed basins, a 22-year record, and anything shown past 2024 is a straight-line illustration, not a forecast.

We built it with:

• Front end: React 19, TypeScript 6, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS 4, Three.js (WebGL and custom GLSL shaders), Recharts.

• Data pipeline: Python 3.11+, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels (STL), pandas, xarray, pymannkendall.

• Data: NASA GRACE/GRACE-FO, NASA POWER, NASA GIBS, NASA EONET, NOAA PSL climate indices.
dataRefs: NASA GRACE / GRACE-FO JPL Mascon RL06.1M v03 (water storage)
NASA POWER API (temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, sunlight)
NASA GIBS imagery (GPM IMERG, VIIRS, MODIS, AIRS, OMI, GRACE layers)
NASA MERRA-2 reanalysis (the model behind NASA POWER)
NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery (globe textures)
projectRefs: NOAA PSL Dipole Mode Index (Indian Ocean Dipole)
NOAA PSL climate indices (North Atlantic Oscillation)
NOAA/NCEP GFS wind analysis (AWS Open Data)
